report.summary: Reviewed chunk 3 of daedalus/kairos/worktree.py; verified docstring claims about reparse-point handling, remove_tree_no_follow delegation, and allocation bookkeeping; no defects found.

handoff.purpose: Continue _remove_tree_no_follow traversal with reparse-point verification, expose remove_tree_no_follow, and define GitWorktreeManager allocation and containment logic.

symbols.name: remove_tree_no_follow
symbols.note: Public wrapper delegating to _remove_tree_no_follow; not an alias so monkeypatching the private also intercepts this.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager
symbols.note: Manages isolated worktrees; records allocations in memory, stores identity snapshots of repo and ancestors, runs git subprocesses.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager.__init__
symbols.note: Resolves repo_path, initializes in-memory allocations dict, stores repo identity and ancestor identities via no-follow path identity.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager.worktree_root
symbols.note: Property returning the worktree root via _worktree_root_for.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._run_git
symbols.note: Runs git subprocess with capture_output, text, check=True; raises RuntimeError on CalledProcessError.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._alloc_file
symbols.note: Returns JSON file path in alloc dir based on SHA256 digest of worktree key.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._record_allocation
symbols.note: Writes allocation record before git worktree add; includes schema, path, repo, branch, created_ts, plus extra fields.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._write_allocation
symbols.note: Creates alloc dir and writes JSON record to alloc file.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._read_allocation
symbols.note: Reads and validates allocation record; returns None if missing, reparse, unreadable, invalid schema, or path/repo key mismatch.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._refuse
symbols.note: Constructs WorktreeContainmentError with explanation and repo/worktree_root context.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._reach_chain
symbols.note: Returns path chain from worktree_root to target; raises _refuse on ValueError.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._refuse_if_repo_adjacent
symbols.note: Raises _refuse if candidate is within repo or repo is within candidate.

symbols.name: GitWorktreeManager._refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved
symbols.note: Docstring-only in this chunk; actual check not visible. Describes mitigation against checkout move attack.

claims.text: Cached, and allowed to be: nothing is traversed on the strength of it -- `child` is re-classified when it is popped.
claims.why: The code appends child to pending without traversing; the walk loop pops and re-classifies each entry via _is_reparse_point and entry.is_dir(follow_symlinks=False).

claims.text: Also cached, also safe: os.unlink removes a link rather than following it, so the worst case is a loud failure.
claims.why: The else branch calls _force_unlink(child); os.unlink does not follow symlinks, so removing a link is safe; failure would raise an exception.

claims.text: Children before parents: a parent is always popped before its children are queued, so its index is lower.
claims.why: The walk pops a directory, queues its children, so the parent is appended to directories before its children; the loop iterates reversed(directories), thus children (higher indices) are processed first. This matches the comment.

claims.text: RE-VERIFIED PER DIRECTORY. Every entry here was classified when it was POPPED, which for the first one drained is the ENTIRE walk ago, and os.rmdir resolves its path argument through a reparse point in an intermediate component exactly as os.scandir does.
claims.why: The loop calls _verify_reachable(directory) before _force_rmdir(directory), re-verifying each directory just before removal. The claim about os.rmdir reparse behavior is consistent with the code's defensive re-verification.

claims.text: An unverified drain therefore lets a junction renamed over an already-drained subdirectory redirect every remaining rmdir out of the tree. Measured, 3/3, end to end through cleanup_worktree: 3000 empty directories removed inside a stand-in primary checkout, reported as success.
claims.why: The measured attack and success are not observable in this chunk; the code does implement per-directory verification, but the empirical claim cannot be confirmed here.

claims.text: Not repaired by unlinking the link: this directory was emptied by the walk above, so whatever is here now is not what was emptied, and the link is not the manager's to delete. Refuse, and report the tree as partially removed.
claims.why: The code raises WorktreeRemovalRace with a message stating the directory became a reparse point and the tree is partially removed.

claims.text: Exists so other modules that must delete a directory candidate code could have reached do not have to import a private, and do not reach for shutil.rmtree because the safe thing looked internal.
claims.why: The function is public and delegates to _remove_tree_no_follow, providing a safe public entry point.

claims.text: The one caller outside this module today is the default pytest gate's scratch directory (:mod:`daedalus.spine.attempt`), which is created in %TEMP% under a predictable daedalus-gate- prefix while candidate code is running as this same user.
claims.why: No caller information is present in this chunk; the claim refers to another module and cannot be verified here.

claims.text: Deliberately delegates rather than being aliased, so a test that monkeypatches _remove_tree_no_follow also intercepts this path.
claims.why: The function body calls _remove_tree_no_follow(root, guarded_ancestors=guarded_ancestors), so monkeypatching the private will affect this path.

claims.text: The ONLY thing :meth:`reap_branches` is allowed to act on. In memory on purpose: the on-disk allocation directory is candidate-writable ... so a record on disk is an attacker-supplied string, not evidence.
claims.why: self._allocations is initialized as a dict in memory; the comment explains the trust model. The claim about reap_branches is not directly checkable here, but the in-memory store is as described.

claims.text: What the primary checkout WAS when this manager was made, NO-FOLLOW. Compared again before every unattended recursive delete -- see _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved.
claims.why: self._repo_identity = _path_identity(self.repo_path) is set in __init__; _path_identity is described elsewhere as no-follow. The comparison in _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved is not in this chunk but the identity storage matches.

claims.text: ...and what every directory the checkout is REACHED THROUGH was. A leaf-only check is bypassed by moving the checkout's PARENT instead of the checkout (measured: 40/40 work files destroyed, leaf identity still matching, because the leaf was being read through the junction that had replaced its parent).
claims.why: self._repo_ancestor_identity is a list of (parent, _path_identity(parent)) for each lexical ancestor, matching the described ancestor tracking. The measured attack is uncheckable, but the data structure exists.

claims.text: CALIBRATED AT CONSTRUCTION, deliberately: it records whatever is there and later demands only that it be UNCHANGED. It must never refuse a machine's layout ... so "is a reparse point" is not the question asked of an ancestor. "Is it the same object it was" is.
claims.why: The ancestor identities are captured at construction from the current layout, and the comment explains the calibration policy. The later comparison is in _refuse_if_the_primary_checkout_moved, not visible here, but the construction matches.

claims.text: Written BEFORE ``git worktree add`` runs. Ordering matters for crash-safety: anything that can exist on disk must already have a record, otherwise a crash mid-``add`` leaves a directory that cleanup would (correctly, but uselessly) refuse forever.
claims.why: The docstring describes ordering; the code itself does not enforce the ordering, but the comment is a statement of intent. The function writes the record as described.

claims.text: Step 3 of :meth:`_require_allocated_worktree` checks this chain once, before the decision; :func:`_remove_tree_no_follow` re-checks it on every directory it opens, because "checked once, before" is exactly the stale classification that let a repository be deleted.
claims.why: The docstring references other methods; _reach_chain returns the chain as described. The claim about _remove_tree_no_follow re-checking is consistent with the per-directory verification seen in the first part of this chunk.

claims.text: ``[worktree_root, ..., target]`` -- what ``target`` is reached through.
claims.why: The function returns _chain_between(_lexical(self.worktree_root), _lexical(target)), which should produce the chain from root to target.

claims.text: Refuse an unattended recursive delete if the checkout is not where it was.
claims.why: The function body is not present in this chunk; only the docstring. Cannot verify the implementation.

claims.text: A MITIGATION, NOT A CLOSURE. The attack it is aimed at is the one no reparse check can ever see, because no reparse point is involved: candidate: os.rename(<primary checkout>, <worktree>/moved_in). Every containment check then passes honestly ... and the whole checkout is destroyed with cleanup returning success (measured, this box, 3/3).
claims.why: The attack description and measurements are not observable in this chunk; they refer to behavior outside the visible code.

claims.text: WHAT IT CATCHES: the checkout being moved (or replaced by something wearing its name) between this manager being constructed and a cleanup running.
claims.why: The docstring describes the intended function; the implementation is not in this chunk.

claims.text: Three checks now stand where one did, and none of them is decoration: 1. repo_path MUST NOT BE A REPARSE POINT ... 2. THE LEAF IDENTITY, no-follow ... 3. THE ANCESTOR IDENTITIES, no-follow, calibrated at construction.
claims.why: The __init__ code sets _repo_identity and _repo_ancestor_identity, and uses .resolve() on repo_path, which prevents reparse points in the resolved path. The checks themselves are in the missing body, but the data needed is present.

claims.text: WHAT IT DOES NOT CATCH, so nobody reads more into it than is there: ... a filesystem with no st_ino. Checks 2 and 3 disable themselves there ... Check 1 still holds at the leaf; NOTHING holds on an ancestor.
claims.why: The behavior on zero inode is in the missing implementation; not observable here.

claims.text: Refusing leaks the worktree (and, in the attack, leaves the checkout alive inside it). That is the correct direction: a leak is recoverable by hand, a deleted checkout is not.
claims.why: This is a policy statement about consequences; the refusal behavior is in the missing function body.
